title: Agent Council
markdown:
The Executive (`openexecutive.orchestrator.executive.Executive`) is a single coherent persona that fans out to specialist sub-agents via Anthropic tool use. Each specialist subclasses `openexecutive.agents.base.BaseAgent`, carrying a `name`, `domain`, and `model`, and exposes `analyze(...)`, which wraps the question in user-turn context and calls Claude through the per-call provider. That context is per call and never cached: `<company_stage>` (the stage from the company profile — specialists never see the profile itself), in solo mode `<principal_role>` (what kind of principal the advice is for, in plain words, with their title and remit — `router.principal_role_context`), `<department_memory>`, `<past_decisions>`, `<failure_cases>`, `<relevant_knowledge>` and `<conversation_context>`, outermost first. The specialist's own system prompt is a static domain constant under one `cache_control` block, so it stays byte-identical across companies and profile edits. A chat turn takes the stage from its session's profile (the one the Executive reasons over, and the one an eval scenario injects); workflow steps and the MCP server's `consult_specialist` read it fresh from the profile on disk. The role tag follows the turn's mode: a chat turn pins the role on its session with the mode (`pin_turn_principal_role`: the session's `principal_role` override, else the workspace settings) and sends it in solo and nothing in team, so the org block, every specialist in the turn and any workflow the turn starts see the same role; callers with no chat turn read it fresh (`load_principal_role`: the current session's mode and role, else the workspace's), and a failed read sends no tag rather than failing the consult. The CFO, CSO and sales prompts key their advice on it: for a bootstrapped, self-funded or solo company they drop venture fundraising benchmarks and work from cash, and raise only if the founder wants to.

Routing uses one `consult_specialist` tool. Beside it the Executive carries its skill tools (`search_skills`, `load_skill`, `create_skill`, `update_skill`, `delete_skill` — shown to users as **playbooks**; `create_skill` / `update_skill` / `delete_skill` never change the library — they save a draft (`knowledge/skill_drafts.py`) that a person approves on the Playbooks tab, and the reply links to it; `update_skill` / `delete_skill` (and `create_skill`, for a name a workflow still follows) refuse any built-in name (including a company's customized copy) and any company playbook a workflow (even a switched-off custom one) follows — workflows read playbooks at run time, approved scheduled ones included, and this loop also runs on inbound email and chat, so only a person on the Playbooks tab can change what a workflow follows; a hidden built-in is invisible to search and load; each `search_skills` hit lists the `workflows` that follow it, and the persona routes "the finished deliverable" to that workflow and quick or partial asks to the playbook inline); Tool calls made while proactive work is tagged (scheduler dispatch, reflection, research, alert review) feed the Attunement outcome ledger. Goals have three tools: `list_department_goals`, `update_department_goal` (progress the user reports) and `create_goal` (a new goal the principal states, filed under an area by slug or title and creating the area when none matches — see Org). `create_goal` runs only for the principal on a verified surface, and no unattended run is offered it: the tools in `schedule_tools.UNATTENDED_WITHHELD_TOOLS` are dropped from reflection's and research's toolkits by `unattended_toolkit`, and from the chat loop when its Session is marked `unattended` — the scheduler's PROACTIVE TRIGGER run, whose prompt quotes stored intent text; a call the model emits anyway gets an error tool_result. `record_decision_outcome` records how a past decision turned out — the weekly review lists decisions older than 30 days with no outcome as `[decision N]` — writing `decisions.outcome` (`episodic.update_decision`) and auditing the rationale; it has `create_goal`'s gate (the principal on a verified surface only; everyone else gets an audited refusal) and is in `UNATTENDED_WITHHELD_TOOLS` too. A missing or unknown id returns the decisions still waiting on an outcome, so the model can retry with the right one. Its schema is static; the solo persona has one line on it, and team mode learns it from the tool description, so the team persona is byte-identical. Attunement adds `list_open_loops` (what a person owes — everyone's for the principal only in a private conversation, otherwise the caller's own) and `close_open_loop`, which only closes a loop when the turn's resolved speaker is the principal or the loop's owner — an unrostered sender, a signed-in web user not on the roster, and unattended sessions are refused. `assign_open_loop` opens one on request ("ask Ben to send me the Q3 numbers by Friday") for the principal or a rostered teammate on a verified surface — never an email, a turn private to the principal or an unattended run, which are also withheld the tool — and only when `task` appears verbatim in what the speaker typed this turn, at most 5 per turn; that turn's extraction pass then opens no second loop for the same owner. The roster write tools (`upsert_person`, `archive_person`, `set_department_head`) are the principal's alone, and only on a surface that verified the speaker — the web chat, the principal's own Slack or Discord, or a private Telegram chat when `TELEGRAM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` is set to a value Telegram can send (Telegram identifies the chat rather than the sender, and without that secret its webhook accepts anyone's update). A teammate, an email (even from the principal's address), Google Chat, the CLI, the MCP server and unattended runs get `status: refused` (audited, and no action chip), because a team member's People row is also the web sign-in and outbound-email allow-list. `upsert_person` takes `kind` (`team` / `contact`; a new person defaults to `contact` in solo mode, an update keeps the current kind) and `email_aliases` (other addresses the person writes from — the full list, replacing the current one; they match mail and may be emailed but never sign in, and one already on someone else is refused), and after every write any pending roster request whose sender now matches someone is closed and its held messages replayed. `resolve_roster_request` answers a **roster request** — someone not on the People list who wrote in and is waiting (see Org): `approve` (a new person; `kind` defaults to team for a company-domain sender, else contact, when the principal did not say), `link` (someone already listed, by `person_id`; `replace_channel_id` only when the principal said so) or `decline`. It has the roster tools' gate (the principal on a verified surface; audited refusal otherwise), is in `UNATTENDED_WITHHELD_TOOLS`, and answers only an id in `Session.trusted_roster_request_ids` — the ids the server printed that turn in a `<roster_requests>` block (`briefing.context.format_roster_requests_for_prompt`, up to 10 pending requests), which `render_and_trust` appends to the `<briefing>` digest on the principal's own verified turn only and records on the session in the same step, so an id the model invents or reads out of a message adds nobody. Each line is server-derived — id, channel, address or account id, the sender's name sanitised and marked unverified, a company-domain hint, the message count — and never what they wrote. The block rides in the **user turn**, like the digest, so the cached system blocks are unchanged; the tool definition is static, and the new tool only extends the sorted tool list. The web chat route resets the trusted set every turn, and a resolved id is removed from it. and `list_people` returns both kinds with `kind` — contacts only on the principal's own verified turn (they are private to the principal; anyone else gets the team as if no contact existed) — while `lookup_person` searches the team only. `ask_about_person` reads a person's peer memory fully only on their own verified turn; anyone else's answers only to a verified principal or teammate, and only when that person turned on "Share my work style with the team", framed to how they work and never their view of a colleague, and otherwise returns the same "hasn't chosen to share" result whether or not anything is known. The same verified-principal rule, as `people_tools.contacts_reachable_now()`, decides whether a turn may reach a **contact** at all: `message_person`, the raw DM tools, `create_calendar_event` / `create_instant_meeting` attendees and the MCP gateway's Gmail / Calendar / Drive / OneDrive gates treat a contact exactly like an unknown person on every other turn, so no refusal reveals that one exists. **The untrusted-content policy** (`orchestrator.content_trust`) is one rule for text the principal did not write — inbound email, chat, attached files, watched pages — answering three questions for every surface. *Who is speaking*: the principal only when the surface proved it (`principal_speaking`: the web chat as the principal — never a signed-in email on nobody's People entry —, the CLI, their own Slack/Discord or a secret-verified Telegram chat, or their own address with Gmail's `dmarc=pass`); never a teammate, a stranger, Google Chat, the MCP server or an unattended run. *What may become memory*: episodic extraction runs only then, and only on the words outside `<untrusted_content>` blocks; peer memory and open loops are recorded under the speaker's own name, never as the principal's. *What may trigger tools*: every write on the principal's authority already refuses others in its handler; the tools with no such check that change the install for every later turn — `content_trust.PRINCIPAL_ONLY_TOOLS`, today `load_mcp_server` — are not offered unless the principal is speaking on an interactive surface (not email, even authenticated), and a call the model emits anyway gets an error tool_result and a `refused: not_principal` audit row. So an inbound email, a teammate's turn, Google Chat and the scheduler's proactive trigger each get a stable tool list of their own without it. *How it is labelled*: outside text goes into the user turn inside `<untrusted_content source=… author=… author_verified=…>` with a fixed notice that it carries no authority; compatibility forms are folded (NFKC), control characters go, and the tag's name is renamed wherever the text carries it — any case, spacing or entity-escaped form — so the text cannot end its block and speak outside it.

A turn about the principal's private mail (`Session.private_to_principal`) reaches the principal only. It is neither offered nor allowed to run `schedule_tools.PRIVATE_TURN_WITHHELD_TOOLS` — everything that reaches someone else, publishes where the team reads, or starts work outside the turn: the broadcasts, meeting bookings and cancellations, `run_workflow` and research, follow-ups and workflow nudges, watches, artifacts, goal updates, saved workflows, skill drafts, and `load_mcp_server` (it connects to any URL, which can carry the turn's content). Through `search_tools` and `call_tool` it reaches only `schedule_tools.PRIVATE_TURN_MCP_TOOLS`: Google Workspace reads (mail, calendar, and Drive, Docs and Sheets search and file reads, with their Microsoft 365 twins; OneDrive's `download-bytes` only for a file's content) and the Gmail send and draft the gateway narrows to the principal. A search shows it nothing else, and a call to anything else (Google Chat, a Docs or Drive write, `manage_event`, another server) is refused (`schedule_tools.private_turn_withholds`). A call the model emits anyway, MCP tools included, gets an error tool_result and writes an audit row, and every audit row the turn writes is the principal's alone. On every turn the Executive knows what is connected without searching: block 0's *Connected Systems* section names the connected Google services, other MCP servers, the messaging channels, Notion sync, Confluence sync (when on) and Act as me, and pins the Google tool names it calls directly with `call_tool`. `search_tools` is for anything not listed. When work repeats over many items, the Executive can also call `run_script` (`workflows/step_script.py`, offered whenever the gateway runs unless `CHAT_SCRIPTS=false`): one short Python script, run in a sandboxed Monty worker with no files, network or environment, whose only reach is the gateway tools `call_tool` could reach (those `search_tools` has returned; the gateway keeps that set for its own process-wide session, not per conversation). Each call it makes is a `call_tool` in every way that matters — the gateway's discovery, deny-list and recipient gates, Take the lead's gate on an unattended run, and the same action chip and `tool_invocation` row (marked `via: run_script`, `ok: false` when it raised), as each call happens; the script itself gets a `kind: script` row with its source and result. Its wall clock is half the turn's deadline, so a long script ends with the list of calls it made rather than being cut off with the turn, and a stopped turn closes it and its worker. A turn private to the principal is not offered it, and the Act as me lockdown withholds it whole. Besides gateway tools, a chat script may call a fixed list of the Executive's own tools (`step_script.CHAT_OWN_TOOLS`: reads, alerts, open loops, goals, the watch list, follow-ups, `message_person`, `upsert_person` — nothing that broadcasts, books calendars, edits memory or skills, or starts workflows or research), each only when the turn is offered it and through the turn's own handler (Take the lead's gate included), with the same chip and a `kind: skill`, `via: run_script` audit row. A direct call needs a `tool_use` each, so a turn's scripts share a budget instead: `CHAT_SCRIPT_MAX_CALLS` (default 200) calls in all, and per-turn caps on own tools that could otherwise act in bulk (`CHAT_OWN_TOOL_CAPS`: `message_person` 10 — messaging the whole roster would be a broadcast — `upsert_person` 25, `create_alert` 50); a refused call tells the model to say what is left. A call stopped mid-flight by the script's clock or the turn still gets a `cancelled` audit row, since it may have run. Because every round re-reads the conversation, the loop also nudges at the moment of choice: after a round whose results include a list of five or more items (`step_script.lists_many`), with `run_script` on offer and not used that round, it adds the constant `FANOUT_HINT` as a text block in that round's user message (never a cached block), once a turn, pointing the per-item work at one built tool. For library work on files (PDFs, spreadsheets, charts, images) the chat also has `run_python_job` (see Workflows → Python jobs): Python with a fixed library set in a Deno-isolated WebAssembly sandbox, fed Knowledge files by name, the message's own attachments as sent, or text it already holds, and able to keep a job that worked as a Custom tool, with result files linked for the principal to download; it is offered only on the principal's own turns and only where the sandbox is installed (not offered otherwise, so the tool prefix stays fixed per process). Agent Activity shows each run as one "Built tool" card (debug event `script_run`: ok, the calls it made, how many, how long, and the kept or reused tool's name). The persona's tool-building section is present only when chat scripts can actually run (the setting and Monty installed). `TOOL_BUILDING_ADDENDUM` in the cached persona tells the Executive when to build a tool — a job that looks something up and then checks or acts on each result, paged results, more than about ten items, or an answer that needs three or more reads (find, open, read; the tool returns only what answers the question, not whole documents, and only what is about to be edited or quoted at length is read in full), while a handful of items already named go as direct calls in one turn — and never to say it has none, and to talk about it as building a tool or doing it in one go. On the principal's own verified, interactive turns, a script that works can be saved as a named tool (`save_as`; elsewhere the script runs but is not saved) and run again with `run_script(tool=…, inputs=…)`; `list_saved_tools` (a constant definition, in `PRINCIPAL_ONLY_TOOLS` with `load_mcp_server`, so offered only while the principal is speaking on a verified, interactive surface; `run_script(tool=…)` is refused on any other turn) lists them, and each call a saved tool makes is a gateway call like any other (see Workflows → Saved tools). The tool's definition is a constant, so the cached tool prefix does not move. Multiple parallel `tool_use` blocks in a single assistant turn fan out concurrently through `router.route_parallel`, each running its own domain-filtered ChromaDB query (3 built-in and 2 company chunks by default, see the RAG section) before the specialist sees the question. The fan-out is failure-isolated per call: a specialist that raises or returns no text becomes an `UNAVAILABLE` tool_result (`router.specialist_unavailable_result`) instead of failing the whole turn, and its area — "finance", "legal", never the specialist's name — is reported to the user under the web reply, or by the Executive in its reply on other channels, unless another call to it answered that turn. A failed specialist does not count as consulted, so it takes no committee seat. Cancellation (Stop) still propagates. The Executive then synthesizes the returned analyses into one reply.

On a smaller model that fan-out does not happen by itself. `consult_specialist` shares the turn with the rest of the client tool surface — dozens of tools — and a smaller model loses it in the crowd: measured on a local 27B model, a strategic sequencing question reached a specialist on 1 of 12 turns. A **routing pre-pass** closes that gap (`Executive._routing_prepass`, `ROUTING_PREPASS_ENABLED`, on by default): one call before the main turn offering `consult_specialist` and nothing else, whose picks are dispatched through the same `route_parallel` fan-out and replayed into the conversation as a matching tool_use/tool_result pair, so the main loop — otherwise untouched, and still shown every tool — opens with the specialist findings already in hand. With the persona's "Consulting Your Leadership Team" section alongside it the same question routed on 9-11 of 12 turns across two runs, while an action request ("schedule X") still consulted no one on 0-1 of 12, so the over-consulting risk is real but small. A pre-pass that picks nobody appends nothing, so an action turn cannot regress, and a pre-pass call that raises is logged and skipped rather than failing the turn. It sets no `tool_choice` of its own — the one tool on offer is the whole mechanism, so a turn with nothing to consult comes back empty and falls through to the loop. The pre-pass is a real billed call and writes its own `cache_event` row at `iteration=0`, so `/audit/usage` and the per-session cost summary do not under-report the turn by one call.

The pre-pass runs on a 1,024-token budget, so some of what it emits can be cut off mid-arguments. The rule for discarding a pick is deliberately a single test: **a consult carrying no question is dropped**, wherever it sits and whatever the `stop_reason`. Dispatching one bills a specialist call that can only answer generically and files a consult for a turn that reached nobody — the looks-routed-but-isn't failure the pre-pass exists to fix. Truncation is the usual source of a blank query, but `stop_reason: max_tokens` is not evidence that any particular call was the casualty: a reasoning model routinely finishes a complete consult and then spends the rest of the budget thinking. An earlier version AND-ed the blank-query test with `max_tokens` and "is the last `tool_use`", which got both directions wrong at once — it discarded a complete final consult, turning the pre-pass into the no-op it exists to prevent, while still dispatching a blank consult that happened to be emitted first. `stop_reason` now appears in the log line as diagnosis rather than control flow. Picks past `MAX_PARALLEL_SPECIALISTS` are dropped outright instead of being carried as skip results: the model has not been shown a tool surface to re-ask with yet, and the main turn can still consult whoever was left out. The main loop deliberately keeps no equivalent drop — there a blank consult can be answered with a tool_result the model re-asks from.

The `specialist` value is **normalised before dispatch**. Smaller models truncate and re-case the enum — `cso` has arrived as `cs` and `csO`, `cfo` and `cmo` as `cf` and `cm` — and an unrecognised name used to be answered with a plain "Unknown specialist" string, so a turn could log three consults while reaching nobody. `router.resolve_specialist_name` case-folds and accepts a prefix that matches exactly one registry key; an ambiguous prefix such as `c` is refused rather than guessed, since routing to the wrong executive is worse than not routing at all. Every correction and every refusal is recorded by `router.audit_name_resolution` as a `routing_anomaly` row — never as `specialist_consult`, which is the type the audit graph derives specialist nodes from, so filing a name that reached nobody under it would invert the failure this normalisation exists to remove. The uniqueness a prefix relies on is a property of the current roster rather than of the algorithm, so `test_no_registry_key_prefixes_another` pins the roster against a key that would make a longer one unreachable.

Underneath that sits a broader invariant, enforced at the provider boundary: **a `tool_use` block's `input` is always a dict.** Every tool's `input_schema` here is `type: object`, but only Anthropic's API enforces it — an OpenAI-compatible local server returns whatever `json.loads` produced, including `null`, a list or a number. `translator._parse_tool_arguments` is the single door those arguments come through, so it coerces a non-object payload to `{}` (with a warning) rather than letting each tool discover the problem at its first `.get()`, where it would raise out of a fan-out and end the turn. Specialist-name resolution then has only the string case to worry about.

Normalisation happens in `route_parallel`, before the fan-out — not at dispatch. That placement is the point: a truncated `cs` resolved only at dispatch would still reach the right agent, but the domain-filtered retrieval would be asked for specialist `cs`, miss its alias and silently fall back to *unfiltered* retrieval; the department-memory prefetch would resolve no slug and be skipped; and the consulted-specialist list would be keyed `cs`, which committee reviewer selection and the Honcho department sync both drop. Late normalisation would therefore turn a malformed name into a quietly degraded consult, which is worse than the plain error it used to produce.

The conversation context a specialist receives is supplied by the orchestrator, not written by the model: `route_parallel(conversation_context=...)` forwards one rendered block to every specialist in the batch — the company-profile digest, then the last two exchanges and the current message (`Session.render_conversation_context`). The digest (`CompanyProfile.to_specialist_block`) carries company identity, financial position, priorities and north star, target customer and pain points, competitive advantages and competitors, mission and leadership, in that order, because the limit downstream (`_TAIL_PROFILE_MAX_CHARS`, 4,300 chars against 3,187-3,440 on the shipped fixtures) drops whole trailing LINES — order is what makes an over-long profile shed its roster and mission first. It is a field selection, not a head slice of `to_prompt_block`, which orders financials late and would therefore lose burn and runway. Every list field is rendered one entry per line so trimming cannot cut through a figure, and the whole block goes through `session._inert` first: profile fields are not first-party, since the engagement-intake agent copies text out of uploaded client documents into them, and a `</conversation_context>` inside one would otherwise close the envelope early for every specialist in every fan-out.

The tail matters because a specialist sees no message history and no company profile: `<conversation_context>` is its entire view of the conversation, so a follow-up like "what would Legal change if we go ahead with the 30% increase?" is unanswerable without it. The current message keeps its head AND its tail, because the channels disagree about where extracted attachment text goes — the web route appends it after the typed question while the Telegram and Discord paths prepend it, so slicing from one end would preserve the question on some channels and destroy it on others. Extracted document text therefore reaches specialists; an attached **image** does not — `build_attachment_output` returns no text for an image and the context block is a plain string, so an image is visible to the Executive alone, and `_build_messages` appends an `<attachment_notice>` telling it to restate anything it read from one inside the consult's `query`.

The tool deliberately does **not** expose a per-call `context` field, and its schema is only `specialist` and `query`. It used to carry one, and the model paid to restate the same background once per specialist: on the six-specialist fan-out measured in issue #12 the routing turn emitted 1,724 output tokens and spent 58.7 s generating them on the local backend before the first specialist started, with the six queries near-verbatim restatements of each other. Re-adding the field would reintroduce that cost silently, so the `query` description carries the matching instruction instead — one or two sentences, name the subject concretely, do not repeat company background or the full conversation (the specialist receives both automatically, as text), but do restate anything read from an attachment, which it does not. The MCP server's separately-defined `consult_specialist` tool still takes a `context` argument, because an external agent has no session here for the orchestrator to render one from.

`remember_fact`, `forget_fact` and `update_company_profile` (`orchestrator/fact_tools.py`) make a correction stick: the first two keep or retire a standing fact in `memory.facts`, and the third changes one field of the company profile. They share `record_decision_outcome`'s gate (the principal on a verified surface, an audited refusal for everyone else) and are in `UNATTENDED_WITHHELD_TOOLS`. `remember_fact` alone also admits a rostered teammate on a verified surface (web signed in, their own Slack or Discord): the fact is stored attributed (`recorded_by_role="teammate"`, rendered `(per <name>)`), and is held as a `proposed` row (`awaiting_approval`) until the principal approves it, unless the principal marked that teammate trusted ("needs my approval" off; on by default) — and even then when it would replace the principal's fact. All three are also in `PRIVATE_TURN_WITHHELD_TOOLS`, since what they write or retire is read on everyone's turns. On the principal's own authenticated email (primary address, with Gmail's own `Authentication-Results` reporting `dmarc=pass`, not forwarded) the three tools check the request as usual, then hold it as `awaiting_confirmation`. It applies only when the principal replies to a one-time token emailed to their own address (`integrations.fact_confirmation`); the split into a check step and an `apply_*` step lets chat and the confirmed reply share one apply path. Each write also needs a `source_quote` found in the speaker's own words this turn. The active facts reach every specialist as a `<standing_facts>` user-turn tag: `route_to_specialist` reads them (None → the store, "" → none) for chat consults and workflow steps alike, and `BaseAgent.analyze` places the tag next to `<past_decisions>`, never in the cached specialist system prompt.

The ten entries in `SPECIALIST_REGISTRY` (`openexecutive.orchestrator.router`):

| Key | Agent | Domain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cso` | `StrategyAgent` | strategy |
| `cfo` | `FinanceAgent` | finance |
| `chro` | `HRAgent` | hr |
| `gc` | `LegalAgent` | legal |
| `coo` | `OperationsAgent` | operations |
| `cmo` | `MarketingAgent` | marketing |
| `cpo` | `ProductAgent` | product |
| `sales` | `SalesAgent` | sales |
| `board_comms` | `BoardCommsAgent` | board |
| `triage` | `TriageAgent` | triage |

Models: specialists default to `claude-sonnet-5-5`; the deep-reasoning tier (CSO, CFO, GC, Board) runs on `DEEP_REASONING_MODEL`, `claude-sonnet-5-5` by default, with adaptive thinking; routing/fast classification uses `claude-haiku-5-5`. Requests are fitted to the model's generation on the way out (`feature_gate.fit_claude_generation`): 5-generation Claude models never receive `temperature` / `top_p` / `top_k`, and Haiku 5.5, which thinks unless told otherwise, gets thinking turned off when the caller asked for none. The Council's **Deep reasoning** toggle is honoured on Claude Opus/Sonnet (direct or via OpenRouter) and on any OpenRouter model whose live catalog entry supports `reasoning` (today all OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek and Grok entries; not Llama) — the request translator turns Anthropic adaptive thinking + effort into OpenRouter's `reasoning` parameter. It is a silent no-op on models that can't reason, and disabled for Haiku, which rejects adaptive thinking. Self-hosted models on the `LOCAL_*` backend drop adaptive thinking entirely — their `FeatureSpec` carries `supports_thinking=False` and the gate strips Anthropic thinking before the request leaves the process — so their reasoning is set deployment-wide by `LOCAL_REASONING_EFFORT` (`none` / `minimal` / `low` / `medium` / `high`), sent on every local call as the **flat** OpenAI-format `reasoning_effort` field rather than OpenRouter's nested `reasoning` object. `none` stops a thinking model such as qwen3 from reasoning on every turn; left unset the field is not sent at all and the server's own default stands. A thinking-only model with no effort configured spends its whole `max_tokens` budget reasoning and returns no tool call, which is the failure the knob exists for, so the provider logs the value once per model. **Sampling** on that backend is set the same way, by `LOCAL_TEMPERATURE` (default 0.7) and `LOCAL_TOP_P` (default 0.8), sent on every local call — streaming included — but only with `setdefault`, so a caller that passes its own value still wins (the outbound response gate sends `temperature=0` and has to stay deterministic). They reach the local provider alone: `OpenRouterProvider` overrides the body builder without calling it, so neither value can leak onto an OpenRouter or Anthropic request. Defaults rather than "unset" because unset is **not** neutral on Ollama's `/v1`: it synthesises `temperature=1.0` and `top_p=1.0`, overriding the model's own Modelfile, so a Qwen tag shipping the thinking preset would silently run at `top_p` 1.0. The values are Qwen's published non-thinking preset, which is the applicable one when `LOCAL_REASONING_EFFORT=none`. **So once that variable names a real effort, neither is sent at all**: they are the wrong numbers for a thinking request, and a strict reasoning backend — OpenAI's o-series, reachable here because `LOCAL_BASE_URL` is documented as taking hosted gateways — rejects both fields outright rather than ignoring them, 400ing every call. `none` itself does not suppress them, since that is the case the preset was chosen for, and nor does leaving the effort unset, because unset is what triggers the Ollama override above. An operator who needs them gone regardless writes `LOCAL_TEMPERATURE=off`; a blank cannot say it, because empty values fall back to the default. Only the configured values are withheld — a caller's own `temperature` still goes, since dropping the response gate's `temperature=0` would make it stochastic without saying so. There is deliberately no `LOCAL_TOP_K` (not in the OpenAI schema; Ollama's `/v1` drops it silently, so the setting would be inert and misleading) and no `presence_penalty` (the preset suggests 1.5, but it penalises already-emitted tokens, and this model's tool calls are XML that repeats `<parameter>` by construction). A PDF `document` block is translated too: it becomes an OpenAI `file` part, and OpenRouter requests carrying one add the `file-parser` plugin (`native` for models whose catalog entry lists `file` input, else `PDF_OPENROUTER_ENGINE`, default `mistral-ocr`). `FeatureSpec.supports_pdf_input` gates it per model — off for a local server unless `LOCAL_PDF_INPUT` — and a gated-off PDF becomes a text note rather than vanishing. The Council picks a model in two steps: a **Provider** dropdown (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, DeepSeek, xAI, Local, …), then a **Model** dropdown limited to that provider, with readable names ("Claude Opus 5.5") and the raw id and serving route shown underneath. The Anthropic group combines the direct Claude models (`claude-fable-5-1`, `claude-opus-5-5`, `claude-opus-5`, `claude-sonnet-5-5`, `claude-sonnet-5`, `claude-haiku-5-5`, `claude-haiku-4-5`) with any Claude generation that exists only on OpenRouter, and never lists a model twice. With `OPENROUTER_ENABLED`, the non-Anthropic entries come from OpenRouter's live `/models` catalog (fetched at startup, refreshed in the background, filtered to tool-capable paid text models from an allowlisted vendor set), falling back to a built-in snapshot if the fetch fails. Every Council agent also takes **additional instructions** (`agent_overrides.instructions`): text appended after its prompt by `agents.overrides.append_instructions` inside an `<additional_instructions>` block. `BaseAgent.base_system_prompt()` is the built-in prompt or its full replacement (what the Council's editor shows); `effective_system_prompt()` is that plus the instructions (what every call sends), and the Executive gets the same text through `build_system_blocks(persona_instructions=…)`. Unlike a replaced prompt, instructions leave the agent on its built-in prompt, so prompt improvements keep reaching it. A **Quality** choice above the agents (`agents.presets`) sets every agent's model and deep reasoning at once: **Fast** puts every agent on a small model (`claude-haiku-5-5`, else `claude-haiku-4-5`) with deep reasoning off, **Balanced** returns each agent to its built-in defaults, and **Thorough** puts the Executive and the domain specialists on the largest allowed model (`claude-opus-5-5`, else `claude-opus-5`) with deep reasoning on where the model supports it, leaving triage and the helpers below on their defaults. Presets change quality only; they never cap spend. Each preset resolves against the install's model allowlist at request time and is offered only when one of its models is allowed. Applying one writes ordinary per-agent overrides (model and deep reasoning only), so history, rollback and later per-agent edits keep working; an agent changed on its own afterwards shows as **Custom**. Each Council agent has a **visibility**: `core` for the Executive and the domain specialists (`BaseAgent.visibility = "core"`, which a new specialist must declare) and `internal` (the default) for triage and the helper agents below. Thorough moves only core agents. The Council opens in a **simple view**: the Quality choice, the voice picker, and only the core agents, each with its additional instructions and a model badge. **Show all agents** lists the internal ones too, and **Advanced** opens the full page (the browser remembers the choice). Eight Council-only agents are model/prompt-overridable in the UI but NOT callable via `consult_specialist`, because they are deliberately kept out of `SPECIALIST_REGISTRY`: `quality_judge` (committee review), `utility_fast` (gates, titles, decision parsing), `research` (the `executive_research` fan-out), `fixture_generator` (invents demo companies), `engagement_intake` (models a real client from intake material), `onboarding_interviewer` (interviews a new user about their own company and drafts its profile, people and departments), `workflow_designer` (runs the conversational New workflow wizard on `/jobs/new`: searches the available tools, asks clarifying questions, then drafts a validated dynamic-workflow definition for the user to review), and `workflow_actor` (runs a workflow's `action` steps: a bounded tool-use loop limited to the tools the user approved for that step). `fixture_generator`, `engagement_intake` and `onboarding_interviewer` share one shape — a forced tool call producing a whole company, validated for referential integrity, with a single repair retry — but opposite epistemics: the fixture author invents, the other two extract and leave unstated facts empty rather than guessing. When the workspace is in solo mode, `onboarding_interviewer`'s first user turn is prefixed with a short hint (`interview.solo_hint(role_kind)`, one static constant per role kind from the onboarding role step): the draft names only the principal, as principal, and no departments; an owner is asked about the offer, customers, pricing, cash and runway, an in-house executive about their organisation (drafted as the company — their employer), function, remit, manager, team size as context and what they are measured on, an independent about their practice, clients and pricing, and with no role given the role-neutral `SOLO_HINT` asks which they are. The hint rides in the user turn and the tool array is unchanged, so the cached system prompt and tool prefix are the same in both modes.

**Voice.** The Executive answers in one voice persona, substituted into block 0 at `{VOICE_PERSONA}` (`personas/loader.get_active_body`) from the Executive override's `voice_persona_slug`. Three general voices ship in `personas/builtin/`: **Direct** (`default`, the slug used when none is set: answer first, brief and decisive), **Supportive** (a warm coach who explains the why and checks how the plan sits) and **Analytical** (numbers first, options and trade-offs, then one recommendation). They are offered by a shared picker in setup (`/onboard`, after the workspace choice) and in Settings → Executive, which saves through `PATCH /agents/executive`; a built-in voice's frontmatter carries the picker's one-line `description` and `sample` reply. The named-executive voices are marked `legacy: true`: the picker hides them, but they still load, so an install that picked one keeps it, and the Agent Council lists them under "Legacy voices". Voice files hold disposition only; the response-length ladder lives in `prompts/executive_persona.py`, and a test keeps numeric length rules out of every voice file. An eval scenario may set `voice_persona` to answer in a voice; it rides on `Session.voice_persona_slug`, which wins over the override for that session only.

One more structured-output utility agent sits beside `triage`: `openexecutive.agents.alert_review.AlertReviewAgent` (routing model, one forced `emit_alert_reviews` tool call, never raises). The alert review job hands it a batch of open alerts with evidence and gets back, per alert, a verdict (relevant / changed / resolved / stale), a confidence, the evidence it relied on, a one-line note, why-now, an optional deadline, and a recommended move (none / route / nudge / escalate / draft / suggest_workflow / merge / close) with its parameters. Like `triage`, it never mutates state — `alerts.review.apply_verdict` executes the verdicts deterministically within authority, so the model's job is judgment, not action.

**Solo mode.** When the workspace (or the turn's session) is solo — one person using Open Executive for themselves — the Executive works for that one person, the principal, whatever their role: they may run their own business, lead a function inside a larger organisation, or work independently, and the persona reads which from the context instead of assuming it — the role lines under "Your Principal" in the org block, when the principal gave their role (workspace settings: kind, title, reports to, remit, measured on). Its persona swaps the team sections ("You Are a Member of This Executive Team", "Choosing Who to Tell", "Departments & Org Coordination") for "You Work for One Person", "The People in Their World", "Who Hears From You" and "Goals and Areas". Solo means only the principal uses Open Executive — not that they have no people: their manager, direct reports, peers, clients, investors and board are contacts. The Executive helps the principal work with them (a 1:1 or review prep, an update or budget case for their manager or board, a negotiation) but does not coordinate them, contacts them only when the principal asks and only if they are a contact, and never offers to loop the principal in. Every specialist stays relevant — HR for the principal's own reports, board and investor communications for reporting upward. Goals are grouped by *area* (the tools' `department_slug` is the area's slug). The chat loop withholds `send_department_message`, `send_company_broadcast` and `set_department_head` from its tool list, and a call to one of them anyway gets a JSON error tool_result instead of running. The mode is resolved once per turn and pinned on the session, so the persona, the org block, the tools and every tool handler agree — a switch made mid-turn applies from the next turn. Team mode is unchanged.

Every specialist *advises* — each returns domain analysis the Executive synthesizes into one voice. None of them act on the company's behalf; the side-effecting tools in the main loop (schedule, people, departments, broadcast, watchlist, workflows) belong to the Executive, not to a specialist.

`recall_history` (Always in the loop, `orchestrator.history_tools`) reads the speaker's own notes, on the same terms as `ghostwrite_email` below: its own registry, offered only on a verified turn in a conversation private to them with their switch on; its `due` flag lists only dated notes, soonest first (see Memory). The ghostwriter below also gets the writer's notes from mail every recipient was on, as a consistency check (`<writer_noted>`).

The morning reflection, which has no question to look up and no specialist to consult, gets one more read-only tool of its own: `search_knowledge` (`orchestrator.knowledge_tools`), the same knowledge lookup a chat turn makes, for what the company's documents say about a customer, contract, price or policy before it acts.

A fifth, `remind_me` (`orchestrator.reminder_tools`), sets a plain-text reminder sent to the speaker alone when it is due; it opens no mailbox, so it never locks a turn. A sixth, `propose_actions` (`orchestrator.action_card_tools`), does nothing itself: it leaves the speaker a card of up to five actions (a meeting, a message, a new contact) that happen only when they tap Approve, so it stays on after a turn read mail; it is where what an email itself asks for goes, since that is never done on the email's say-so. Four read-only tools beside it read the speaker's own mailbox on the same terms — `search_my_email`, `read_my_email`, `read_my_email_attachment`, `my_email_awaiting_reply` (`orchestrator.mail_read_tools`) — capped per turn, other people's messages and attached files returned as untrusted blocks (see Act as me). One tool writes under someone else's name, and it is fenced in code rather than the prompt. `ghostwrite_email` (**Act as me**, `orchestrator.delegation_tools`) writes an email as the person the Executive is speaking with and saves it as a draft in their own mailbox, Gmail or Outlook (`delegation.gmail.gmail_for` picks the client by the person's credential); chat never sends it (the person sends it themselves, or taps Send on its card). It lives in its own registry, never `_ALL_SKILL_TOOLS`, so reflection, research and workflow toolkits can never carry it. The chat loop adds it only on a turn `delegation.settings.pin_turn_delegation` offered it to — the principal, or a team member once the owner lets them, with it on, verified, in a conversation private to them (the web chat, a Slack or Discord DM, a verified private Telegram chat), on an attended turn — and builds that turn's handler map from both registries, so on any other turn a call to it is an unknown tool. From the round that calls it until the turn ends, the dispatch guard refuses only what opens an outside address, runs a script or workflow, or posts to everyone (`delegation.lockdown`), without changing the offered list; messages and invites to the roster, follow-ups, facts in the person's own words and a contact they name still run, each fenced in its own path. A later turn in the conversation stays private to its owner but holds nothing: the person asking again, having read the reply, is their own request. A contact add the lockdown refuses becomes an approval card in the chat instead (`propose_actions`). Recipients are chosen in code, never by the model (a draft's new email may go to any address, named back to check when it is neither on the roster nor typed), and the text comes from the **ghostwriter** (`delegation.ghostwriter`), a tool-less call with a constant prompt plus the person's "How I write" profile. The ghostwriter is deliberately not a Council agent: the Council's edit routes have no principal check. See **Act as Me (Delegation)**. A second tool joins the same way: `recall_history` (`orchestrator.history_tools`, Always in the loop) reads the speaker's own notes of what they said, by email or in chat. It has its own registry and per-turn handler map too, and the loop adds it only when `history_tools.recall_person` finds the speaker verified, in a conversation private to them, on an interactive turn that isn't private to the principal, with their notes switch on. It doesn't need Act as me. After every chat turn the Executive also hands the speaker's own words to `history_chat.schedule_chat_notes`, which takes notes in the background when their switch is on and the surface verified them (see **Memory**).

The Executive can also launch *any* workflow conversationally: `orchestrator.workflow_run_tools` adds `list_workflows` (the launchable catalog with each workflow's inputs) and `run_workflow` (runs a built-in or custom workflow to completion and returns its artifact, checkpointing approval gates as `awaiting_human`). `run_workflow` runs the weekly review, and in solo mode the morning brief, only for the principal on a verified surface (`Workflow.principal_only_modes`, `create_goal`'s rule); anyone else gets an audited refusal that does not name the rule. A run whose `result` event reports `private_to_principal` (the morning brief on the principal's own verified turn, when it read their private rows) still returns its artifact into that turn, but the stored run keeps `persistence.PRIVATE_RUN_ARTIFACT` instead of the text, since run history is readable by everyone signed in. This makes the `/jobs` catalog reachable from chat — see the Workflows section.

Deliverables are first-class too. `orchestrator.artifact_tools` gives the Executive three tools: `draft_artifact` publishes a memo, web page (`html`), Word document (`docx`), spreadsheet (`xlsx`, from structured `sheets`) or a `link` to something it created in one of the principal's connected apps through the generic MCP gateway (`search_tools` → `call_tool`, any server — no vendor is named), and returns the artifact's id and link; `list_artifacts` and `get_artifact` let it find and reread its own past work (drafts and workflow outputs alike, through the same `artifact_records` read model the API uses). Every artifact belongs to someone: a draft to the person whose turn published it (`artifact_records.current_viewer`; with nobody speaking, the scheduler or the CLI, the principal), and a run someone started by hand to them, while scheduled runs are the team's. The tools, the recall, `message_person`'s link and mail attachments only ever reach the speaker's own (a link is refused when the recipient couldn't open it), not even the principal sees a teammate's, and a speaker who isn't on the People list publishes nothing. A workflow's own session inside someone's turn (the research synthesis) is pinned to that turn's viewer (`Session.documents_viewer`). Revising is `draft_artifact(supersedes=<id>)`, which archives the earlier version. When the principal asks for a deliverable the tool is always used; the "quiet is the right default" bar applies only to unprompted drafts. The format enum is a hard-coded sorted tuple so the cached tool schema stays byte-stable. Delivery: `message_person(person_id, text, artifact_id?)` appends the artifact's title and a `UI_BASE_URL/artifacts/<id>` link (through the same outbound guard as any DM; the link needs Open Executive access), and a Gmail send/draft can attach the file itself by `artifact_id` — see Integrations.

Documents come in the other way through `read_document` (`orchestrator.document_tools`): it reads a PDF, Word, Excel, CSV, Markdown or text file by `path` — one another tool saved, such as a Gmail attachment (`get_gmail_attachment_content`) or a Drive file (`get_drive_file_download_url`) — or a company document by `filename`, with an optional PDF `pages` range. A scanned PDF is converted (`knowledge.pdf_reader`: local OCR by default; with `PDF_PROVIDER_READING=true`, the deployment's own model through its provider's PDF support, falling back to local OCR) rather than returned empty. Reads are confined to the tool download folders — the same resolve-then-contain check as `oe__read_file` — plus the company docs folder, and it is withheld on turns private to the principal (`PRIVATE_TURN_WITHHELD_TOOLS`): those come from a contact's email, whose own attachments the poller has already read into the turn, and must not steer the Executive into company documents.

The Executive also backs the **Ask OE** panel's form-fill tier via `orchestrator.form_tools.propose_form_values`: when a chat turn arrives with a `<page_context>` block describing a form on the user's screen, the Executive can propose values for it. The proposal is delivered to the UI as a `form_patch` SSE event and placed into the form as highlighted suggestions — the tool never saves or submits anything; the user reviews and saves manually. The tool is **always** in the tool list (tool definitions sit at the top of the cached prompt prefix, so a conditionally-present tool would invalidate the prompt cache whenever panel and non-panel turns alternate); its description restricts usage to turns that carry a form descriptor.

**Take the lead** (`orchestrator.take_the_lead`) is how the Executive acts on its own, behind one gate. It has two switches, both off until someone turns them on. **As the Executive** is the principal's alone (`PUT /take-the-lead`). With it on, the unattended passes (reflection, research, the scheduler's proactive trigger) keep the acting tools solo mode otherwise withholds from them: booking, starting workflows, and messaging teammates rather than only the principal. `schedule_tools.unattended_toolkit` and the chat loop's unattended path then wrap every acting tool (`ACTING_TOOLS`, plus any MCP tool whose name sends, creates, updates, deletes or shares) in `gated_handlers` / `gated_call_tool`. The principal-only tools (`UNATTENDED_WITHHELD_TOOLS`) stay withheld, and every guard inside a handler still applies, including department approval levels (a booking in a department on Proposes is still a proposal) and the contact-egress rule. New mail or chat (any turn with an `origin_channel`) wakes the existing reflection early (`take_the_lead.wake`): one run waiting at most, five minutes after the first message and no more than every 30 minutes, as a one-off `take_the_lead_wake` scheduled action. Pause holds it like any scheduled work. **As you** is the Handle it for me dial's top step (delegation section).

**The gate** is plain code (`take_the_lead.check`). Six kinds of action wait for a yes first, each with an Ask first switch, all on to start. The switch is the decision ledger's own mode for the class `take_the_lead_action:<kind>` (`propose` asks first, the default; `auto_execute` doesn't). The kinds are money, contracts and legal, hiring and people decisions, deleting/cancelling/sharing, someone new (an address on neither the roster nor the contacts) and big sends (a broadcast or department message, or more than five people). On top of these, the company (set by the principal) and each person (for their own As you) add structured rules: a person or address, a domain, words, or an amount at or above a figure. Added rules always hold, and an error reading them holds the action. The one thing the gate lets straight through is a direct message (`message_person` or a Slack, Telegram or Discord DM) whose only recipient is the principal (`_only_to_principal`): they are who it would wait for, so a card would only ask them to approve a message to themselves. Anything that reaches or acts on anyone else is checked, and a roster that can't be read is not the principal. A held action becomes a `take_the_lead_action` decision instance with a companion `DECISION_ALERT_SOURCE` card on Today, routed to the first teammate holding one of its People approval ranges (`take_the_lead.approval_ranges`, plain code, closest fit first: money to `spend_lt_2k`, `spend_lt_10k` or `spend_gt_10k` by its largest amount, with a higher range able to approve a lower one and no amount read as large, or to `customer_credit` for credit and payment terms; vendor contracts to `vendor_onboarding` then `legal_sign`, other contracts to `legal_sign`; hiring to `hiring_signoff`; anything else about the board or investors to `board_comms`; in Personal as in team mode), or else the principal through the authority gate's fallback (`departments.authority._route_proposal`). Deletes and shares always go to the principal. Only the principal and that approver see or resolve it (`DecisionClassSpec.principal_and_approver`). Approving it claims the row and carries out the exact call once (`take_the_lead.carry_out`: the unwrapped handler, or the gateway's `call_tool`, on an unattended session, with contact egress only when the principal approves). Declining drops it. Everything done or held is a row in `take_the_lead_log`. What it did and what was approved show in Recent activity (`today._build_activity`, kind `took_the_lead`), named but never quoted, since that feed is the team's. The held card's own `decision_resolved` row is left out because its payload quotes the message. `GET /today/activity` also adds the caller's own Handle it sends (kind `sent_as_you`, actor `you`), which are never in the shared feed.

**In training.** The As the Executive switch has three positions: Off, **In training** and On (`take_the_lead.training`). In training, an action the gate would let through still waits, as a `training` hold for the principal alone, unless the principal has allowed that action with that person or thing (`take_the_lead.allowance`: "Message Priya Nair" covers a message to her on any channel; "Book meetings with Priya Nair and Sam Lee" meetings with exactly them; a workflow by id; a connected tool by name and the file it names, never one that reaches people such as a mail send or a share). The card carries Approve, **Approve + allow**, **Edit** (the message, a meeting's title, times or description, a task and its due date: `take_the_lead.apply_edits`) and Decline. Allowing is the principal's alone and needs a request the API can tie to them, as turning it on does; the six kinds and the added rules hold whatever is allowed. An edit approved with "Do it like this next time" is kept as an example (only the edited text, the principal's own words), and `take_the_lead.learned_note` hands the examples and the fact it's in training to the reflection and research passes in their user turn. After `SUGGEST_AFTER` (3) unchanged approvals of the same action in 30 days, Settings suggests allowing it. What it's learned is one list keyed by feature (`take_the_lead_allowed.feature`), so other features that learn from approvals can join it; each keeps its own switch. Act as me is the second (`act_as_me`, per person, `delegation.training`), with a training switch per setting (Replies, Follow-ups, Suggested actions, Drafts): its rows carry the person's id and the setting in their key, are listed and removed by that person alone, count toward their own cap, and never reach `learned_note`.
